## What a GLM does

A linear model assumes a normal response with constant variance. Counts and yes/no data break both assumptions. A **generalized linear model** keeps the linear predictor but adds:

- a **family** (error distribution) that matches the data, and
- a **link function** that connects the mean to the linear predictor.

| Response | Family | Link | R call |
|----|----|----|----|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | `glm(..., family = gaussian)` = `lm()` |
| Counts | `poisson` | log | `glm(..., family = poisson)` |
| Overdispersed counts | negative binomial | log | `MASS::glm.nb()` |
| 0/1, presence/absence | `binomial` | logit | `glm(..., family = binomial)` |

GLMs are tested with **likelihood-ratio (LR) χ²** tests instead of F-tests, and fit is compared with **AIC** (lower is better).

## Step 1: Load packages and data

```{r}
#| label: step-1-load
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)       # clean_names()
library(car)           # Anova()
library(MASS)          # glm.nb()
library(performance)   # check_overdispersion(), r2()

g_df <- read_csv("data/galapagos_species_area.csv")

polis_df <- read_csv("data/polis.csv", na = c(".", "")) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  drop_na(paratio, pa)
```

`MASS` has its own `select()`. If you load it after the tidyverse, write `dplyr::select()`.

## Part A: Counts — plant species on Galapagos islands

### Step 2: Look at the counts

For a Poisson variable the variance equals the mean. A ratio far above 1 is **overdispersion**.

```{r}
#| label: step-2-counts
g_df %>%
  summarise(mean_spp = mean(n_species),
            var_spp  = var(n_species),
            ratio    = var_spp / mean_spp)
```

```{r}
#| label: step-2b-plot
#| fig-width: 3.4
#| fig-height: 3
g_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(log(area_km2), n_species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "log(island area, km²)", y = "Number of plant species") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Step 3: Poisson GLM

```{r}
#| label: step-3-poisson
poiss_model <- glm(n_species ~ log(area_km2),
                   data = g_df,
                   family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(poiss_model)
```

### Step 4: Check for overdispersion

```{r}
#| label: step-4-overdispersion
check_overdispersion(poiss_model)
```

A dispersion ratio near 1 is fine. Here it is far above 1, so the Poisson standard errors are too small and its p-values are too optimistic. Switch to a negative binomial.

### Step 5: Negative binomial GLM

```{r}
#| label: step-5-negbin
nb_model <- glm.nb(n_species ~ log(area_km2), data = g_df)

summary(nb_model)
check_overdispersion(nb_model)
```

### Step 6: Test and compare

```{r}
#| label: step-6-test
Anova(nb_model, type = "III", test = "LR")

AIC(poiss_model, nb_model)
```

The negative binomial has a much lower AIC, so it fits far better.

### Step 7: Interpret the slope

Coefficients are on the **log** scale. Exponentiate to get a multiplicative effect:

```{r}
#| label: step-7-interpret
exp(coef(nb_model))
```

Each 1-unit increase in log(area), i.e. a 2.7-fold larger island, multiplies the expected number of species by about `r round(exp(coef(nb_model)[2]), 2)`.

## Part B: Presence/absence — Uta lizards on islands

### Step 8: Look at the data

`pa` is 1 if *Uta* lizards are present, 0 if absent. `paratio` is the island's perimeter-to-area ratio.

```{r}
#| label: step-8-look
polis_df %>% dplyr::select(island, paratio, pa)
count(polis_df, pa)
```

### Step 9: Logistic regression

```{r}
#| label: step-9-logistic
lizard_model <- glm(pa ~ paratio,
                    data = polis_df,
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"))

summary(lizard_model)
```

### Step 10: Test against a null model

The likelihood-ratio test compares the model with an intercept-only model.

```{r}
#| label: step-10-lrt
null_model <- glm(pa ~ 1, data = polis_df, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

anova(null_model, lizard_model, test = "Chisq")
```

### Step 11: Odds ratios and fit

```{r}
#| label: step-11-odds
#| message: false
exp(coef(lizard_model))                  # odds ratios
exp(confint(lizard_model, "paratio"))    # 95% CI for the odds ratio

r2(lizard_model)                         # pseudo-R²
```

An odds ratio below 1 means the odds of presence **drop** as `paratio` rises: each 1-unit increase multiplies the odds by `r round(exp(coef(lizard_model)[2]), 2)`.

### Step 12: Plot the fitted curve

```{r}
#| label: step-12-plot
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
polis_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(paratio, pa)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial)) +
  labs(x = "Perimeter:area ratio", y = "Probability Uta present") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Step 13: Write it up

```{r}
#| label: step-13-numbers
nb_lr  <- Anova(nb_model, type = "III", test = "LR")
liz_lr <- anova(null_model, lizard_model, test = "Chisq")
```

> Plant species richness increased with island area (negative binomial GLM, LR χ²~1~ = `r round(nb_lr[1, "LR Chisq"], 1)`, p < 0.001); a Poisson model was strongly overdispersed.

> The probability that *Uta* lizards were present declined as island perimeter:area ratio increased (logistic regression, LR χ²~1~ = `r round(liz_lr$Deviance[2], 1)`, p < 0.001; odds ratio = `r round(exp(coef(lizard_model)[2]), 2)` per unit ratio, n = `r nrow(polis_df)` islands).

Report the family and link, the LR χ² with df and p, and the effect on the response scale (multiplier or odds ratio).
